items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use the following property to simplify expressions involving expected values:

Content:
> For any random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] and constants [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we have
> [MATH: \textrm E[aX+bY] = a \textrm E[X] + b \textrm E[Y].]

Content:
In other words, the expected value of a sum of scaled random variables equals the sum of the scaled expected values.

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[2X+5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] + 5 \textrm E[Y].]

Content:
Note that the property also works with subtraction:

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[2X-5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] - 5 \textrm E[Y]]

Content:
We can extend this idea to any number of random variables. For example, for any random variables [MATH: X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,] and real constants [MATH: a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n], we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[a_1X_1+a_2X_2+\cdots+ a_nX_n]= a_1\textrm E[X_1]+a_2\textrm E[X_2]+\cdots +a_n\textrm{E}[X_n],]
or more concisely,
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right] =\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \textrm E[X_i].]

Content:
Note that the random variables [MATH: X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,] are not required to be independent.

| [MATH: y] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: f(y)] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{16}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{8}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{16}] |

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: X_i] be the [MATH: i]th score obtained from the fair die, and let [MATH: Y_j] be the [MATH: j]th score obtained from the unfair die. Also, let [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] represent the scores obtained from a typical throw of the fair and unfair die, respectively.

Then, we need to calculate

[MATH: \textrm E\left[ \sum_{i=1}^2 X_i + \sum_{j=1}^4 Y_j \right].]

Using the properties of expected value, we have

[MATH: E[∑_(i = 1)^(2)X_{i} + ∑_(j = 1)^(4)Y_{j}]|= ∑_(i = 1)^(2)E[X_{i}] + ∑_(j = 1)^(4)E[Y_{j}]; = 2E[X] + 4E[Y],]

where the last equality above is true because [MATH: \textrm E[X_i] = \textrm E[X]] and [MATH: \textrm E[Y_j] = \textrm E[Y]] for all [MATH: 1\leq i \leq 2,\: 1\leq j\leq 4.]

The expected values of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are calculated as follows: [MATH: E[X]|= 1 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 2 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 3 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 4 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 5 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 6 ⋅ (1)/(6) = (7)/(2); E[Y]|= 1 ⋅ (1)/(4) + 2 ⋅ (1)/(16) + 3 ⋅ (1)/(4) + 4 ⋅ (1)/(8) + 5 ⋅ (1)/(4) + 6 ⋅ (1)/(16) = (13)/(4)]

Hence, we get

[MATH: \textrm E[2X+4Y]=2\textrm E[X]+4\textrm E[Y]= 2\cdot \dfrac{7}{2}+4\cdot \dfrac{13}{4} =20.]

Content:
The expected value of the product of two independent random variables is equal to the product of the expected values. So, if the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[X\cdot Y] = \textrm E[X]\cdot \textrm E[Y].]

Content:
For example, if we know that [MATH: X] are [MATH: Y] are independent, and that [MATH: \textrm E[X]=2] and [MATH: \textrm E[Y]=3], then
[MATH: E[X ⋅ Y]|= E[X] ⋅ E[Y]; = 2 ⋅ 3; = 6.]

Content:
When working with the expected value of a product of random variables, it's important to check that the variables are independent. The formula above is not true if [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are not independent.

Content:
More generally, if the random variables [MATH: X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n] are mutually independent, then

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[X_1\cdot X_2 \cdots X_n]=\textrm E[X_1]\cdot \textrm E[X_2]\cdot\ldots\cdot \textrm E[X_n],]
or more concisely,
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[ \prod_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \prod_{i=1}^n \textrm E[X_i],]

where [MATH: \prod] is the product operator.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can use the following property to simplify expressions involving expected values:

Content:
> For any random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] and constants [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] we have
> [MATH: \textrm E[aX+bY] = a \textrm E[X] + b \textrm E[Y].]

Content:
In other words, the expected value of a sum of scaled random variables equals the sum of the scaled expected values.

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[2X+5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] + 5 \textrm E[Y].]

Content:
Note that the property also works with subtraction:

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[2X-5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] - 5 \textrm E[Y]]

Content:
We can extend this idea to any number of random variables. For example, for any random variables [MATH: X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,] and real constants [MATH: a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n], we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[a_1X_1+a_2X_2+\cdots+ a_nX_n]= a_1\textrm E[X_1]+a_2\textrm E[X_2]+\cdots +a_n\textrm{E}[X_n],]
or more concisely,
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right] =\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \textrm E[X_i].]

Content:
Note that the random variables [MATH: X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,] are not required to be independent.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Expected Value of a Sum of Random Variables

Example Prompt:
Compute [MATH: \textrm E[5X-2Y]] if [MATH: \textrm E[X]=1] and [MATH: \textrm E[Y] = 2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For any random variables [MATH: X,Y] and any constants [MATH: a,b,] we have

[MATH: \textrm E[aX+bY] = a \textrm E[X] + b \textrm E[Y].]

Therefore,

[MATH: E[5X − 2Y]|= 5E[X] − 2E[Y]; = 5(1) − 2(2); = 1.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Expected Value of a Sum of Random Variables in Context

Example Prompt:
Andrea has two dice. One of them is fair, and the other is not. The rolls of the unfair die follow the probability mass function [MATH: f(y)] shown in the table below. What is the expected sum of the outcomes of [MATH: 2] throws of the fair die and [MATH: 4] throws of the unfair one?

| [MATH: y] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: f(y)] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{16}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{8}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{16}] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: X_i] be the [MATH: i]th score obtained from the fair die, and let [MATH: Y_j] be the [MATH: j]th score obtained from the unfair die. Also, let [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] represent the scores obtained from a typical throw of the fair and unfair die, respectively.

Then, we need to calculate

[MATH: \textrm E\left[
\sum_{i=1}^2 X_i + \sum_{j=1}^4 Y_j
\right].]

Using the properties of expected value, we have

[MATH: E[∑_(i = 1)^(2)X_{i} + ∑_(j = 1)^(4)Y_{j}]|= ∑_(i = 1)^(2)E[X_{i}] + ∑_(j = 1)^(4)E[Y_{j}]; = 2E[X] + 4E[Y],]

where the last equality above is true because [MATH: \textrm E[X_i] = \textrm E[X]] and [MATH: \textrm E[Y_j] = \textrm E[Y]] for all [MATH: 1\leq i \leq 2,\: 1\leq j\leq 4.]

The expected values of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are calculated as follows:
[MATH: E[X]|= 1 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 2 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 3 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 4 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 5 ⋅ (1)/(6) + 6 ⋅ (1)/(6) = (7)/(2); E[Y]|= 1 ⋅ (1)/(4) + 2 ⋅ (1)/(16) + 3 ⋅ (1)/(4) + 4 ⋅ (1)/(8) + 5 ⋅ (1)/(4) + 6 ⋅ (1)/(16) = (13)/(4)]

Hence, we get

[MATH: \textrm E[2X+4Y]=2\textrm E[X]+4\textrm E[Y]= 2\cdot \dfrac{7}{2}+4\cdot \dfrac{13}{4} =20.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Expectation of a Product of Random Variables

Content:
The expected value of the product of two independent random variables is equal to the product of the expected values. So, if the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[X\cdot Y] = \textrm E[X]\cdot \textrm E[Y].]

Content:
For example, if we know that [MATH: X] are [MATH: Y] are independent, and that [MATH: \textrm E[X]=2] and [MATH: \textrm E[Y]=3], then
[MATH: E[X ⋅ Y]|= E[X] ⋅ E[Y]; = 2 ⋅ 3; = 6.]

Content:

Content:

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[X_1\cdot X_2 \cdots X_n]=\textrm E[X_1]\cdot \textrm E[X_2]\cdot\ldots\cdot \textrm E[X_n],]
or more concisely,
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[ \prod_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \prod_{i=1}^n \textrm E[X_i],]

where [MATH: \prod] is the product operator.
